title: How To Handle Students Who Need Your Attention
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin addresses the exhausting problem of students who constantly seek attention, arguing their neediness is a learned behavior reinforced by adults who never made them handle small problems themselves. He describes how such students become dependent, turning minor issues like a papercut or a comma choice into demands for adult intervention, and explains this is rooted in a normal childhood desire to be the center of attention taken to an unhealthy extreme. His fix is two SCM-foundational strategies: first, enforce the classroom management plan so students must raise a hand and wait rather than blurting out or following the teacher around, using the resulting pause to build self-reliance and responding with encouragement phrases rather than answers; second, push hard for independence by teaching with extreme clarity, requiring proof of understanding, and then withdrawing help almost entirely so students are forced to rely on their own judgment. He argues the payoff extends well beyond attention-seeking, producing gains in confidence, academic ability, and especially maturity.
points: Attention-seeking behavior is learned, not innate — students have discovered that the 'squeaky wheel' strategy of never taking no for an answer gets them what they want.
Enforce hand-raising and seat rules so needy students can't blurt out or follow you around; the pause this creates does the work of building self-reliance.
When you do respond to a needy student, provide encouragement rather than the answer: phrases like 'You got this' or 'Go back and read it again.'
Push hard for independence by teaching with extreme clarity, requiring proof of understanding, then shifting total responsibility to students with minimal or reluctant help.
The payoff of breaking learned helplessness goes beyond less clinginess — Linsin claims it produces visible gains in confidence, academic ability, and maturity within weeks.
quotes: They follow you around and pull on your hem. They ask a zillion questions and expect your personalized attention.
Students who crave attention mean well. They’re not trying to annoy you or get under your skin. The truth is, their behavior is learned.
They get their way by never taking no for an answer. They’ve discovered that the squeaky-wheel strategy works.
If needy students are unable call out and unable get up from their seats without raising their hand and asking permission, then you limit their ability to reach you.
Force them to rely on their own wits until they realize it’s futile to ask you and that they can indeed trust their own judgment.
Behavior, confidence, and academic ability will all improve. Most of all, however, is maturity, which will skyrocket. They’ll become different people in a few weeks.
